Q10. The authors described the chirality of the deterministic switching in affected by the in-plane
external field. What defines this chirality?
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful question and for the opportunity to
clarify the meaning of “chirality” as used in this work. Achieving field-free SOT switching with
tunable chirality is indeed the central focus of our work. Below, we provide a detailed explanation of
the underlying mechanism.
In the present manuscript, chirality refers to an operational and device-level sense to denote the
deterministic polarity of current-induced magnetization switching, i.e., whether a given current
direction drives the perpendicular magnetization from zz or from -z+z. It should be noted that,
to align with the well-established hallmark characteristic feature of deterministic SOT-driven
switching, where the switching polarity is modulated by changing the direction of the in-plane external
field in the field-assisted SOT switching. We have replaced the terminology “chirality” with
61
“polarity” throughout the main text and in the following responses, although we use this term to define
the switching polarity in our unique IMA/PMA structure for field-free case. This revision ensures
consistency with the terminology used in the existing literature.
The physical quantity that defines this switching polarity is the in-plane symmetry-breaking field
acting on the PMA layer during SOT switching. In conventional PMA systems, such symmetry
breaking is typically provided by an externally applied in-plane magnetic field. In our heterostructure,
this role is instead played by an internal effective field arising from interlayer exchange coupling with
the IMA component, which thus enables field-free SOT switching (Nat. Commun. 10, 233 (2019)60).
Specifically, the magnetization direction of the IMA layer can be preset by an external in-plane
magnetic field during initialization. Once preset, the IMA layer generates a remanent interlayer
exchange field with a well-defined in-plane direction, which breaks the in-plane symmetry of the PMA
layer. The sign of this effective field, relative to the current direction, uniquely determines the
deterministic switching polarity. Consequently, reversing the preset in-plane magnetization of the IMA
layer reverses the direction of this internal effective field and, correspondingly, reverses the switching
polarity.
Therefore, the polarity discussed in this work is a field-defined and controllable switching polarity,
determined by the preset orientation of the IMA magnetization through interlayer exchange coupling,
rather than a manifestation of chiral magnetism.

The authors have made a substantial effort in response to the first-round reviews. The additional
experiments, particularly the XRMR measurements, extended switching characterization, and control
analyses, represent a nontrivial experimental investment and significantly strengthen the empirical
foundation of the manuscript. In this regard, I find the breadth of new data largely satisfactory.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the positive assessment of our revision efforts and for
acknowledging that the additional experiments have significantly strengthened the manuscript’s
empirical foundation.
My remaining concerns are not about the sufficiency of the data, but rather about how firmly some
conclusions are framed relative to what the experiments directly establish. In several places, the
manuscript presents interpretations in a way that feels more definitive than necessary. I believe the
paper would be strengthened by a more matter-of-fact tone that explicitly acknowledges alternative
interpretations and explains why the authors favor the scenario they propose.
For example, the XRMR measurements provide strong evidence for the coexistence of in-plane and
perpendicular magnetic components and for a depth-dependent weighting of these contributions.
However, statements suggesting that these data exclude impurity phases or uniquely define a sharp
spatial separation along the film normal seem overstated. A more accurate description would
emphasize that the data are consistent with a graded magnetic structure, with near-surface regions
contributing more strongly to the in-plane signal and deeper regions showing enhanced perpendicular
sensitivity, while acknowledging the limits of angular averaging and depth resolution. Similarly,
clarifying whether the applied in-plane and out-of-plane fields are sufficient to fully polarize the
respective components would help readers assess the robustness of the interpretation.
Response: We appreciate the insightful comment regarding the interpretation of our XRMR data. We
agree that our original phrasing was overly definitive. In the revised manuscript and Supplementary
Information, we have adopted a more measured tone. Specifically, we now describe the data as being
consistent with a graded magnetic structure, where IMA contributions are dominant near the surface
and PMA contributions increase with depth toward the interface, rather than claiming a sharp spatial
separation. Furthermore, we have clarified that the applied in-plane (±150 mT) and out-of-plane (±300
mT) magnetic fields are sufficient to fully polarize the respective components, ensuring the robustness
of our analysis. We believe these revisions significantly enhance the clarity and rigor of our
interpretation.
These revisions have been made in Supplementary Information S9:
“For out-of-plane measurements, the magnetic field was applied normal to the sample surface and
reversed between positive and negative directions, with a maximum field of ±300 mT. These applied
field are expected to be sufficient to fully polarize the respective components, thereby ensuring a robust
magnetic contrast for the XRMR analysis……By combining the penetration depth at grazing incidence
with the observed magnetic asymmetry and hysteresis loop measured at 9.5° under an in-plane
magnetic field (Fig. S9e), the data are most consistent with a model in which the near-surface region
is dominated by IMA components……The data support a picture of a graded magnetic structure where
IMA contributions are stronger near the Fe GeTe surface, while PMA contributions increase with
4 2
depth toward the Bi Te interface.”

probe, and the manuscript should avoid language that implies unambiguous spatial localization of this

We believe this addition makes the discussion more transparent and complete. We again thank the

The clarification that the observed SOT switching is partial is helpful. However, the statement that
incomplete switching is generally characteristic of two-dimensional magnets is too broad. The
conditions under which switching is partial or near-complete remain an open and actively studied
question, and Fe GeTe is a comparatively underexplored system in this context. Framing the observed
4 2
behavior as part of this broader, unresolved landscape would be more accurate and more interesting.
Response: We thank the reviewer for correcting our previous over-generalization. We agree that
characterizing partial switching as a "general feature" of 2D magnets was imprecise. In the revised
manuscript, we have refined this statement to reflect that achieving full magnetization reversal remains
a significant practical challenge in the 2D limit, consistent with reported efficiencies in similar systems.
The relevant sentence in the main text now reads: “These values are consistent with reported SOT
efficiencies in other two-dimensional magnetic systems (e.g., ~20%) and reflect the practical challenge
of achieving full magnetization reversal in the two-dimensional limit.” This revision places our
observations within the broader context of current research on switching completeness in emerging 2D
magnetic systems.
Finally, the proposed exchange-spring-like picture is intriguing and plausible, but it remains a model
rather than a directly proven mechanism. Presenting it explicitly as such, and incorporating the new
control data and schematics into the supplementary information, would make the argument clearer and
more transparent.
Response:We thank the reviewer for the constructive suggestion to clarify the nature of the exchange-
spring-like picture. Accordingly, we have revised the relevant section in Supplementary Information
S7. The text now explicitly presents this concept as a plausible and self-consistent physical model that
is consistent with our data, rather than a directly proven mechanism. The supporting control data and
schematics have been incorporated therein to enhance the clarity and transparency of the argument.
Overall, I am supportive of publication after moderate revisions focused on interpretive tone and clarity
rather than additional experiments. Adopting a more open and explicitly comparative narrative would
significantly strengthen the manuscript.
Response:We appreciate the reviewer's support for publication and the valuable guidance to improve
the manuscript’s clarity and narrative. We will revise the text to ensure a more open and comparative
tone as suggested.
